title: AI Knows Best? The Paradox of Expertise, AI-Reliance, and Performance in Educational Tutoring Decision-Making Tasks
venue: LAK 2026: 16th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference
extended_summary:
This paper examines how people evaluate the correctness of tutor praise responses when assisted by AI-generated decision support. The central question is whether human-AI collaboration improves accuracy relative to humans working alone, and how explanation style affects performance, time, and reliance on AI. The authors focus on two explanation modalities: textual reasoning and inline highlighting.

The study uses 216 tutor-response examples drawn from a tutor training system. Ground-truth labels were created by two experienced tutors and a PhD learning scientist, and a GPT-4-based model produced labels and explanations. In the user study, 95 participants were recruited: 47 professionally trained tutors and 48 Prolific participants. Participants completed a counterbalanced online experiment with five conditions: no AI, AI label only, label plus reasoning, label plus highlighting, and label plus both reasoning and highlighting. They first received a training module on effective praise and then judged 20 items per condition.

Results show that AI assistance improved human accuracy relative to no AI, but human-AI collaboration still underperformed the AI-only baseline. Novices from Prolific benefited more from AI because they tended to follow AI suggestions, while experienced tutors more often overrode correct AI advice, producing more under-reliance. Textual reasoning reduced under-reliance when the AI was correct but increased over-reliance when the AI was wrong; inline highlighting had little measurable effect. Neither explanation style improved overall accuracy, and both increased time spent. The paper concludes that explanation design in tutor-facing decision support should aim to better calibrate trust and reduce both over- and under-reliance.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed experimental study with counterbalanced within-subject conditions and clear statistical testing, but it is not a randomized field trial in K-12 classrooms and uses a simulated tutoring judgment task rather than actual instructional outcomes. The participants are mixed professionals and Prolific respondents, so ecological validity for K-12 tutoring support is limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The study shows statistically significant but task-specific effects, including modest accuracy gains from AI assistance and meaningful changes in reliance patterns, but it does not demonstrate student learning gains or classroom-level impact. The primary contribution is diagnostic evidence about human-AI decision support rather than direct educational impact.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated decision support for evaluating tutor praise responses, including binary correctness labels plus textual reasoning and inline-highlight explanations shown to human tutors

finding.finding_summary: AI assistance improved human decision accuracy versus no-AI baseline, but the human-AI team still underperformed the AI-only baseline (AI accuracy=0.8; human-AI conditions significantly better than no-AI, F(1,471)=6.83, p=.009, ηp²=.014). Novices (Prolific) generally outperformed experienced tutors overall (overall accuracy 0.747 vs 0.712; t=-2.302, p=.0236), suggesting expertise did not translate into better judgment in this task.
finding.measure: Accuracy on tutoring decision-making judgments (correctly labeling tutor praise as effective/ineffective)
finding.effect_size: ηp²=.014; t-tests reported overall group difference d=0.470
finding.std_deviation: Tutor overall SD=0.088; Prolific overall SD=0.057

finding.finding_summary: AI explanations increased time spent per task. Repeated-measures ANOVA showed significant main effects for inline highlighting (F(1,57)=25.74, p<.001, ηp²=.311) and text reasoning (F(1,57)=19.12, p<.001, ηp²=.251), with a significant interaction (F(1,57)=18.26, p=.001, ηp²=.243), indicating the explanation features added processing time rather than reducing it.
finding.study_size: n=95 total; time analysis after IQR filtering reported on n=58 for within-subject ANOVA
finding.std_deviation: Tutor no-label SD=3.95s; Prolific no-label SD=3.43s; other condition SDs reported in Table 2

finding.finding_summary: Text reasoning changed reliance behavior in both directions: it reduced under-reliance when AI was correct (F(1,94)=8.71, p=.004, ηp²=.085) but increased over-reliance when AI was wrong (F(1,94)=8.81, p=.004, ηp²=.086). Inline highlighting had no significant effect on either under-reliance or over-reliance, suggesting that explanation quality influenced trust calibration more than visual salience alone.
finding.measure: Over-reliance and under-reliance rates in AI-assisted tutoring judgments
